en: To exist in very large numbers; to be plentiful
hook: A-BOUND-less supply: so much that there's no boundary.
story: Abound. To exist in very large numbers. Every June, Sheila's grandmother phones with the same instruction: "Bring empty bags." In the orchards around her house, mangoes abound. Branches bend almost to the ground, every basket on the veranda overflows, and neighbours leave mangoes at each other's doors. Sheila [laugh] fills her bags and still cannot carry them all. Abound shares a root with abundant, from the Latin for overflowing, like a wave spilling over. When things abound, there is more than anyone needs. So, what verb means to exist in huge numbers? ... Abound.

gre.s: Far from being scarce, allusions to the ancient epic ____ in the poet's later work, surfacing in nearly every stanza.
gre.clue: Far from being scarce

example: Hidden jokes abound in the cartoonist's drawings, so careful readers find something new on every page.

en: A state of not caring or feeling any interest
hook: A-PATHY: without (a) feeling (pathos).
story: Apathy. A state of not caring or feeling any interest. Marty spent a month organising his university's blood donation camp. He printed posters, booked doctors, and borrowed tables from the canteen. On the day, only nine students came, while hundreds walked past scrolling their phones. Marty packed up quietly. It was not anger that hurt him; it was apathy. The Greek a means without, and pathos means feeling: apathy is life without feeling. Its opposite is passion, or simply care. So, what word names a complete lack of interest or concern? ... Apathy.

gre.s: Organizers were dismayed by the public's ____; despite months of campaigning, only a handful of people attended the rally.
gre.clue: only a handful of people attended the rally

example: Years of broken promises had bred deep apathy among residents, who no longer bothered to report potholes to the city corporation.

en: Very enthusiastic or passionate
hook: ARDENT: burning with ARDOR.
story: Ardent. Very enthusiastic or passionate. Every Friday morning, Rita's grandfather walks two kilometres to watch the village boys play cricket. He has not missed a match in thirty years. He knows every boy's batting style and shouts advice from the boundary until his voice is hoarse. When the youngest batsman hit his first six, the old man [laugh] threw his cap into the air. He is the club's most ardent fan. Ardent comes from the Latin for burning, the same root as ardour: an ardent fan burns with enthusiasm. So, what word describes someone burning with passion? ... Ardent.

gre.s: Even her most ____ admirers, who had defended every one of her earlier films against hostile reviewers, conceded that her latest effort was a disappointment.
gre.clue: who had defended every one of her earlier films

example: An ardent reader of detective stories, Nusrat had finished every Feluda book before she turned twelve.

en: A strong dislike or disinclination
hook: AVERSION: you AVERT (turn away) your eyes from it.
story: Aversion. A strong dislike. Aaron loves almost every dish except bitter gourd. Since childhood, the sight of bitter gourd on his plate has made him turn his face away. His mother tried frying it crisp, mixing it with potatoes, even hiding it in the dal. Somehow Aaron found it every time. Now he is thirty, and his aversion has not changed at all. Aversion comes from avert, to turn away: when you have an aversion to something, you turn away from it. So, what word names a strong dislike that makes you turn away? ... Aversion.

gre.s: The novelist's lifelong ____ to publicity explains why, despite her enormous commercial success, she has given almost no interviews.
gre.clue: she has given almost no interviews

example: Despite his aversion to early mornings, the new intern reached the lab by six every day to feed the mice.

en: Making people obey by threatening or pressuring them
hook: COERCION: COERCE = FORCE.
story: Coercion. Making people obey by threatening or pressuring them. A garment worker named Tracy was told by her supervisor that unless she signed a paper giving up her overtime pay, she would lose her job. With rent due and a child at home, she signed. Later, a labour court ruled the signature worthless, because it had been obtained through coercion. Think of coercion as force with a threat instead of a fist: to coerce someone is to force them to act against their will. So, what word names getting someone to obey through threats? ... Coercion.

gre.s: The court threw out the confession, ruling that it had been obtained not through voluntary cooperation but through ____, since the suspect had been threatened with violence.
gre.clue: the suspect had been threatened with violence

example: Election observers reported widespread coercion, with villagers warned that they would lose their land if they voted the wrong way.

en: Spread out over a large area; wordy and unfocused (adj.); to spread out (verb)
hook: DIFFUSE: like perfume DIFFUSING through a room — spread thin.
story: Diffuse. Spread out over a wide area; also, wordy and unfocused. Scott's first essay tried to cover climate change, cricket, his grandfather and artificial intelligence, all in five hundred words. It wandered everywhere and landed nowhere. His teacher returned it with one comment: "Too diffuse. Choose one idea." Scott started again. As a verb, diffuse means to spread out, like a drop of ink slowly spreading through water. Do not confuse it with defuse, which means to calm a tense situation. So, what word describes writing so spread out that it has no clear focus? ... Diffuse.

gre.s: Critics complained that the documentary was too ____, touching on dozens of topics without exploring any of them in depth.
gre.clue: touching on dozens of topics without exploring any of them in depth

example: The light from the paper lantern was soft and diffuse, filling the room without casting a single sharp shadow.

en: A difference or lack of agreement between things that should match
hook: DISCREPANCY: the numbers DISAGREE.
story: Discrepancy. A difference between things that should match. At the end of the month, Brittany checked the debating club's accounts. Her ledger said the club had four thousand two hundred dollars, but the bank held only three thousand eight hundred. Her stomach dropped. She went over every page with the treasurer until midnight and finally found it: a donation written in the book but never actually deposited. The discrepancy was explained, and Brittany could breathe again. Discrepancy comes from the Latin for sounding different, like two instruments out of tune. So, what word names a mismatch between numbers that should agree? ... Discrepancy.

gre.s: Investigators grew suspicious when they noticed a ____ between the company's public earnings reports and the figures it had submitted to tax authorities.
gre.clue: grew suspicious when they noticed

example: A small discrepancy between the two lab reports, one listing the sample at 37 degrees and the other at 39, delayed the whole study.

en: Fundamentally different; not able to be compared
hook: DISPARATE: DIS + PARITY. No parity, no equality; completely different.
story: Disparate. Completely different from one another; hard to compare. Andy's GRE study group looked unlikely at first: a shy software engineer, a loud young doctor, a quiet painter, a retired army officer, and a teenage cricketer. They shared no age, no job, and no taste in music. Yet every Saturday they met in a small café, argued, and cheered each other's scores for months. Such disparate people became close friends. Do not confuse disparate with desperate; listen instead for apart: disparate things are worlds apart. So, what word describes things fundamentally different from each other? ... Disparate.

gre.s: The anthology gathers such ____ voices, from medieval mystics to modern rappers, that readers may wonder what unites them.
gre.clue: from medieval mystics to modern rappers

example: The museum's new gallery pairs disparate objects, such as a Mughal coin beside a plastic toy, to show how trade shaped daily life.

en: To wipe something out so that none of it remains
hook: E-RADIC-ATE: pull out by the ROOTS (radix).
story: Eradicate. To wipe something out so that none of it remains. In the early nineteen seventies, smallpox still haunted villages across the Ganges delta. Health workers went house by house, vaccinating families and tracing every case. In nineteen seventy-five, a little girl on a river island became the last person in the world known to catch the deadliest natural form of the disease. She recovered, and smallpox was later eradicated worldwide. Eradicate comes from the Latin for root: to eradicate is to pull something out by its roots. So, what verb means to destroy something completely? ... Eradicate.

gre.s: Public health officials hoped not merely to control the disease but to ____ it entirely, so that no new cases would ever appear again.
gre.clue: so that no new cases would ever appear again

example: The school launched a campaign to eradicate bullying, training older students to step in whenever they saw it happen.

en: To bring a feeling, memory, or image to mind
hook: E-VOKE: call (voke, voice) OUT a memory.
story: Evoke. To bring a feeling, memory or image to mind. Fiona had lived in Toronto for years. One snowy evening, in a small corner grocery, she smelled fresh samosas frying and heard an old love song on the radio. Suddenly she was nine again, sitting beside her grandmother on a rainy afternoon. She [sigh] stood still, eyes wet. The smell and the song evoked her childhood. E means out, and voc means voice or call, so to evoke is to call a memory out. So, what verb means to bring a memory or feeling to mind? ... Evoke.

gre.s: For many people, the smell of rain on dry earth seems to ____ childhood memories more powerfully than any photograph ever could.
gre.clue: more powerfully than any photograph ever could

example: The composer used slow, rising strings to evoke the vast emptiness of the desert at night.

en: Still in existence
hook: EXTANT: still standing, not EXTINCT.
story: Extant. Still in existence. Seth's grandfather, an old scholar, collects hand-copied manuscripts of songs and stories. Many such books were lost to floods, insects and fire. One afternoon, he unwrapped a red cloth and showed Seth a cracked little book two centuries old. "Only three copies are still extant," he whispered. Seth [gasp] held his breath. Extant sounds close to extinct, but it means the opposite: extinct things are gone, while extant things survive. So, what word describes something that still exists today? ... Extant.

gre.s: Although the playwright is known to have written more than forty comedies, only three are ____ today; the rest perished when the theater's archives burned.
gre.clue: the rest perished

example: The oldest extant recording of the folk song was made on a fragile wax cylinder, and it crackles badly.

en: To understand after much thought
hook: FATHOM: measuring deep water — and deep ideas.
story: Fathom. To understand something after much thought. Molly's grandmother could not fathom why anyone would pay eight dollars for a cup of coffee. She turned the receipt over twice, as if the reason might be printed on the back, then [chuckle] asked whether the cup came free. A fathom is also a sailor's measure of depth, about six feet: to fathom something is to reach the bottom of it. We often use it with not, as in I cannot fathom it. So, what verb means to finally understand something puzzling? ... Fathom.

gre.s: Even after decades of study, physicists struggle to ____ the strange behavior of particles at the quantum level, which seems to defy every intuition about cause and effect.
gre.clue: which seems to defy every intuition about cause and effect

example: Rumi could not fathom how his younger sister had solved the puzzle in two minutes when it had taken him all evening.

en: To worry anxiously
hook: FRET: FRETTING like fingers on guitar FRETS, never still.
story: Fret. To worry anxiously. The night before her visa interview, Kayla could not sleep. What if they asked about her funding? What if she forgot her bank statement? She checked her folder five times and paced the room until three in the morning. Finally her mother brought her warm milk and said, "Do not fret. You have prepared well." Kayla smiled and lay down. Fret also means to wear away, like water slowly fretting a stone, which is exactly what worry does to you. So, what verb means to worry anxiously, again and again? ... Fret.

gre.s: Although her doctors assured her that every test result was normal, she continued to ____ about her health, waking at night convinced that something was wrong.
gre.clue: waking at night convinced that something was wrong

example: Coach Rahman told his players not to fret over the lost first set, since the match was far from decided.

en: To hinder or slow the movement or progress of
hook: HAMPER: like carrying a heavy laundry HAMPER while trying to run.
story: Hamper. To slow down or get in the way of progress. Lenny's online classes were going well until load-shedding returned. Every hour the power cut out, his router died, and he missed ten minutes of the lecture. His notes filled with gaps. The power cuts badly hampered his studies. At last his uncle lent him a small battery backup, and Lenny [laugh] cheered when the router stayed on. Picture trying to run while carrying a heavy laundry hamper: whatever hampers you slows you down. So, what verb means to hinder progress? ... Hamper.

gre.s: Language barriers continue to ____ cooperation between the two research teams, slowing what could otherwise be rapid progress.
gre.clue: slowing what could otherwise be rapid progress

example: A sprained ankle hampered the striker for most of the season, and he managed only two goals.

en: Doing things suddenly, without stopping to think first
hook: IMPULSIVE: driven by IMPULSE.
story: Impulsive. Doing things suddenly, without stopping to think. Randy walked into a shopping mall to buy socks. He walked out with a guitar, a gaming chair and a lamp shaped like a puppy, and no money left for the month. None of it was planned; each purchase simply felt right in the moment. That night he ate plain rice and counted his coins. Randy is impulsive. An impulse is a sudden push, and an impulsive person is pushed by every passing wish. Its opposite is deliberate. So, what word describes someone who acts suddenly without thinking? ... Impulsive.

gre.s: Known for weighing every option for months, the cautious director surprised her board with an uncharacteristically ____ decision, announcing the merger the very afternoon it was proposed.
gre.clue: announcing the merger the very afternoon it was proposed

example: In an impulsive moment, Sabrina dyed her hair bright green the night before her cousin's wedding.

en: Can be used in place of each other equally well
hook: INTER-CHANGE-able: can be CHANGED between.
story: Interchangeable. Able to be used in place of each other equally well. When Danny's phone charger broke the night before a trip, he grabbed his sister's from her desk, and it fit perfectly. Their chargers were interchangeable. In English, too, big and large are usually interchangeable. But careful: on the GRE, many words that look similar are not interchangeable. Complacent and confident, for example, mean very different things. Break the word apart: inter means between, so interchangeable things can be changed between one another. So, what word describes two things that can swap places equally well? ... Interchangeable.

gre.s: Though the two terms are often treated as ____, scientists use them to describe quite different phenomena.
gre.clue: scientists use them to describe quite different phenomena

example: On a well-run assembly line the parts are fully interchangeable, so any bolt fits any car of the same model.

en: To grieve over or deeply regret something, often aloud
hook: LAMENT: 'LAME, meant to be better', sad regret.
story: Lament. To grieve over or deeply regret something, often aloud. Twenty years ago, Shannon's grandfather sold the family home in the village to pay for his children's education. It was the right choice. Yet on quiet evenings he still laments it, speaking softly about the two mango trees, the pond where he learned to swim, and the courtyard where his mother cooked. As a noun, a lament is a song or poem of grief, like the slow songs of river boatmen. So, what verb means to express deep sorrow or regret? ... Lament.

gre.s: Many critics ____ the decline of the independent bookstore, mourning the loss of places where readers once gathered.
gre.clue: mourning the loss of places where readers once gathered

example: Long after retiring, the old batsman still laments the easy catch he dropped in a final twenty years ago.

en: Clear and easy to follow; thinking clearly
hook: LUCID: full of LIGHT (lux), crystal clear.
story: Lucid. Clear and easy to understand; also, thinking clearly. Tommy had failed maths twice. Then a new teacher arrived and explained compound interest using one bank account, three years, and the price of a cup of tea. Every step made sense, and Tommy [gasp] suddenly saw the whole picture. Her explanation was lucid. Lucid comes from the Latin lux, meaning light: a lucid explanation lets the light shine through. A person can also be lucid, thinking clearly after confusion or fever. So, what word describes an explanation so clear it is easy to follow? ... Lucid.

gre.s: Despite the complexity of the subject, her ____ explanation allowed even beginners to grasp the theory.
gre.clue: allowed even beginners to grasp the theory

example: Even after the long surgery, my grandfather was lucid enough to joke with the nurses and ask about the cricket score.

en: Motivated only by money; a soldier hired to fight for a foreign army
hook: MERCENARY: works only for MERCHANDISE and money.
story: Mercenary. Motivated only by money; also, a soldier hired to fight for a foreign army. Patients at one private clinic noticed something odd. Whatever their illness, each was told they needed costly scans, more tests, and often surgery. The owner's new car grew shinier, but his patients did not get better. A young journalist named Jake finally exposed him. People called the doctor mercenary. Mercenary comes from the Latin for wages: historically, mercenaries were soldiers who fought for whoever paid them most. So, what word describes someone who acts only for money? ... Mercenary.

gre.s: Critics charged that the consultant's advice was ____, designed less to help her clients than to maximize her own fees.
gre.clue: designed less to help her clients than to maximize her own fees

example: The club's owner was accused of mercenary motives when he sold its best young players to rivals a week after they won the league.

en: An open rebellion against authority, especially by soldiers or sailors
hook: MUTINY: the crew MUTES the captain and takes over.
story: Mutiny. An open rebellion against authority, especially by soldiers or sailors. On a cargo ship in the Bay of Bengal, the crew had gone four months without pay. For weeks the sailors stayed silent. Then one morning, they refused to work, took over the bridge, and kept the captain in his cabin until the owners promised their wages. It was a mutiny. To remember it, picture a mute crew that finally finds its voice: the silent sailors rise in mutiny. So, what word names a rebellion by sailors or soldiers against their commanders? ... Mutiny.

gre.s: Exhausted by months of harsh discipline and dwindling rations, the sailors threatened to ____ unless the captain agreed to turn the ship toward home.
gre.clue: unless the captain agreed to turn the ship toward home

example: When the coach cancelled their holiday for extra training, the exhausted players came close to staging a mutiny.

en: Deeply moving in a way that stirs sadness
hook: POIGNANT: POINTED, it pierces your heart.
story: Poignant. Deeply moving in a way that stirs sadness. At the airport, Preston watched an old man hug his son, who was leaving to work in Malaysia for five years. The father pressed a small packet of homemade cookies into his son's hands and said nothing. Neither could speak. Preston felt his throat tighten. It was a poignant moment. Poignant comes from an old French verb meaning to prick, the same root as pungent: a poignant scene pricks the heart. So, what word describes a moment so moving that it makes you sad? ... Poignant.

gre.s: The film's final scene is quietly ____: the elderly widower, alone in the empty house, still sets out two cups of tea each morning out of habit.
gre.clue: alone in the empty house, still sets out two cups of tea each morning out of habit

example: In the war museum, the most poignant exhibits are ordinary belongings, a pair of spectacles or a child's shoe, left behind by the dead.

en: Dangerously unstable or uncertain
hook: PRECARIOUS: like a CAR parked on the edge of a cliff.
story: Precarious. Dangerously unstable or uncertain. On a city building site, a young worker named Henry stood on a thin bamboo scaffold six floors up, balancing a basket of bricks on his head. He wore rubber sandals and no harness, and below him buses roared past. His mother back in the village prayed for him every night. His position was precarious. The word comes from the Latin for prayer: something precarious is so unsteady that you can only pray it holds. So, what word describes a situation dangerously unstable and uncertain? ... Precarious.

gre.s: With only a single seat separating the two parties, the governing coalition's majority remained ____, liable to collapse with one defection.
gre.clue: liable to collapse with one defection

example: Moving from one short contract to the next, many young researchers lead a precarious life with no job security at all.

en: A hard or awkward situation that is tough to escape
hook: PREDICAMENT: a PREDICTION gone wrong, now you're stuck.
story: Predicament. A hard or awkward situation that is tough to get out of. Owen reached the bus terminal with five minutes to spare, then realised his wallet was gone. No ticket, no money, a dead phone, and his university admission test in another city the next morning. He stood there, wondering whom he could possibly ask. He was in a real predicament. Remember: a dilemma is a hard choice, while a predicament is a hard situation you are stuck in. So, what word names an awkward situation with no easy way out? ... Predicament.

gre.s: Stranded abroad after their airline collapsed, and with no money to buy new tickets, the tourists faced a grim ____ that their embassy was slow to resolve.
gre.clue: Stranded abroad after their airline collapsed

example: Having promised to attend two weddings on the same evening, Ayesha was in a predicament that no excuse could solve.

en: Good at something through training and practice
hook: PROFICIENT: as skilled as a PRO.
story: Proficient. Skilled at something through training and practice. When Nicole joined a software company, she could barely write a program that worked. She practised every night after work, solved hundreds of coding problems, and asked senior colleagues endless questions. Two years later, the newest interns were lining up at her desk for help. She had become truly proficient. Proficient comes from a Latin verb meaning to make progress: you become proficient by progressing step by step. So, what word describes someone skilled through long practice? ... Proficient.

gre.s: Although she had studied Spanish for only a year, she was already so ____ that native speakers often assumed she had grown up in Madrid.
gre.clue: native speakers often assumed she had grown up in Madrid

example: Ayan became proficient at repairing mobile phones after spending two summers in his uncle's shop on Elephant Road.

en: Something you can turn to for help when in trouble
hook: RE-COURSE: the COURSE you turn to when all else fails.
story: Recourse. Something you can turn to for help when in trouble. When Mason's landlord refused to return his security deposit, Mason felt helpless. He could not afford a lawyer. Then a friend told him about a free legal aid clinic run by law students at his university. That clinic became his recourse, and within a month he had his money back. Recourse comes from the Latin for running back: a recourse is what you run back to when trouble comes. Do not confuse it with resource. So, what word means a source of help you can turn to? ... Recourse.

gre.s: Because their insurance policy explicitly excluded flood damage, the farmers found themselves without ____ when the river burst its banks and destroyed their crops.
gre.clue: Because their insurance policy explicitly excluded flood damage

example: With the bank closed for the holiday, Sumon's only recourse was to borrow from a neighbour to pay the hospital bill.

en: To improve by making small changes; to remove impurities
hook: RE-FINE: make it FINE again and again.
story: Refine. To improve something with small changes; also, to remove impurities. Kristen wrote her statement of purpose in one evening and felt proud. Then she spent three weeks refining it: twelve drafts, cutting weak sentences, sharpening examples, and replacing vague words with exact ones. The final version was half as long and twice as strong. Refine means to make fine again and again, the way a sugar mill refines brown sugar until it is pure white. So, what verb means to improve something through careful small changes? ... Refine.

gre.s: Over decades, the craftsmen continued to ____ their techniques, gradually eliminating flaws until their porcelain was the finest in the world.
gre.clue: gradually eliminating flaws

example: Over ten years, physicists refined their measurement of the particle's mass, cutting the margin of error in half.

en: What a person is paid for the work they do
hook: RE-MUNER-ATION: MONEY (munus) given back for work.
story: Remuneration. What a person is paid for the work they do. Rhonda translated a long novel for a big city publisher. When she asked about payment, the editor offered her a free copy of the book and a thank-you in the preface. Rhonda smiled politely, [chuckle] and explained that her landlord did not accept thanks as rent. She wanted proper remuneration. The root is the Latin munus, meaning gift or service: remuneration is a gift given back for your service. Careful, it is remuneration, not renumeration. So, what word names payment for work? ... Remuneration.

gre.s: Many of the volunteers worked for years without ____, motivated not by money but by their deep commitment to the cause.
gre.clue: motivated not by money

example: Many interns at Dhaka's advertising agencies work long hours for remuneration that barely covers their bus fare.

en: Calm, peaceful, and untroubled
hook: SERENE: SERENITY.
story: Serene. Calm, peaceful and untroubled. At dawn, Hope sat alone on the shore of a mountain lake. Mist rested on the green hills, the water lay perfectly still, and the only sound was a distant boatman's oar. After months of city traffic, she [sigh] felt her shoulders loosen. The morning was serene. Serene comes from the Latin for a clear, cloudless sky: a serene mind has no storm clouds in it. A serene person stays calm even in a crisis. So, what word describes a scene perfectly calm and peaceful? ... Serene.

gre.s: In contrast to the frantic, crowded market just outside its walls, the monastery garden remained ____, its stillness broken only by birdsong.
gre.clue: its stillness broken only by birdsong

example: Even as reporters shouted questions at her, the newly elected mayor remained serene, answering each one with a slight smile.

en: Slow-moving, inactive, or lacking energy
hook: SLUGGISH: as slow as a SLUG.
story: Sluggish. Slow-moving and lacking energy. After his colleague's wedding lunch of spiced rice, creamy curry and two helpings of rice pudding, Bill went back to his desk. Every email took twice as long, his eyelids drooped, and his thoughts moved like cold honey. He felt completely sluggish. That year the country's economy was sluggish too, with businesses barely growing. Picture a slug crawling across a garden path after rain: sluggish things move like a slug. So, what word describes someone slow and heavy, with no energy? ... Sluggish.

gre.s: Despite heavy government spending, the economy remained ____, growing at barely one percent for the third straight year.
gre.clue: growing at barely one percent for the third straight year

example: The old laptop had grown so sluggish that opening a single spreadsheet took almost five minutes.

en: Occurring at irregular intervals; scattered
hook: SPORADIC: like SPORES floating randomly here and there.
story: Sporadic. Happening at irregular intervals; scattered. All through one dry March, Melanie's father watched the sky over his jute fields. Rain came only in sporadic showers: a ten-minute burst on Monday, nothing for nine days, then a drizzle one night. He [sigh] could not plan his sowing. When the steady rains finally arrived, the whole family [laugh] ran outside to stand in them. Sporadic comes from a Greek word for scattered, like seeds tossed while sowing; spore shares the root. So, what word describes events that happen only now and then, with no pattern? ... Sporadic.

gre.s: Fighting in the region has been ____ rather than continuous, flaring up unpredictably and then falling silent for weeks.
gre.clue: flaring up unpredictably and then falling silent for weeks

example: Apart from sporadic visits from his nephews at Eid, the old fisherman saw almost no one during the long winter.
